# Long-term causes of the First World War

Historians often group the causes of the First World War into four long-term factors: militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism. In the decades before 1914, the great powers of Europe built up large armies and navies. Germany and Britain competed in a naval race, and both sides believed that a short and decisive war could be won quickly. Military planning, such as the German Schlieffen Plan, assumed rapid mobilisation, which left little time for diplomacy once a crisis began.

The alliance system divided Europe into two camps. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy formed the Triple Alliance, while France, Russia and Britain were linked by the Triple Entente. These agreements were meant to deter attack, but they also meant that a local conflict could quickly draw in several powers. A dispute between two states was no longer only their own affair.

# Imperialism and nationalism

Imperial rivalry also raised tensions. The European powers competed for colonies in Africa and Asia, and crises such as those over Morocco in 1905 and 1911 brought Germany into conflict with France and Britain. Each crisis was solved without war, but each one left behind mistrust and a feeling that the next confrontation could not be avoided.

Nationalism was strong in many countries. In the Balkans, the decline of the Ottoman Empire created new states and new ambitions. Serbia wanted to unite the South Slavs, many of whom lived inside Austria-Hungary. The government in Vienna saw Serbian nationalism as a threat to the survival of its multinational empire. Russia, which saw itself as the protector of the Slavs, supported Serbia. The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 made the region even more unstable.

# The July Crisis

The immediate cause of the war was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. The assassin was a young Bosnian Serb linked to a nationalist group. Austria-Hungary, with the support of Germany, sent Serbia an ultimatum with demands that were very hard to accept. Serbia accepted most of them, but not all, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July.

Russia began to mobilise in support of Serbia. Germany declared war on Russia and then on France, and its invasion of neutral Belgium brought Britain into the war on 4 August. Within a few weeks, a crisis in the Balkans had become a general European war. Historians still debate how much responsibility each government carries, but most agree that the long-term factors made the July Crisis far more dangerous than it would otherwise have been.
